newsitem.title: USA: World Microprocessor market seen doubling by 2000.
newsitem.headline: World Microprocessor market seen doubling by 2000.

text.p: The worldwide market for microprocessors -- the brains of computer systems -- is poised to grow at an 18 percent clip through the year 2000, with industry giant Intel Corp. leading the most profitable segment, according to a computer industry research firm.
In a forecast to be released on Monday, San Jose-based Dataquest projects the market will grow to $33.6 billion in the year 2000 from $14.1 billion in 1995.

Dataquest said the computational complex instruction set computing or CISC segment, which includes the x486 microprocessors used in personal computers is expected to continue to be the most profitable sector of the entire semiconductor industry, producing more than 90 percent of microprocessor revenue, while accounting for less than half of unit shipments.
CISC processors are capable of carrying out complicated computations at the basic, assembly language level.
"The good news is that a pot of gold awaits any vendor able to achieve success in this market," said Nathan Brookwood, an analyst in Dataquest's Semiconductor Applications program.
However, he noted that Intel holds a solid grip on this part of the industry's most lucrative market.

"The bad news (for competitors) is that Intel stands watch over this pot of gold, and any contender must first defeat, or at least, distract, Intel before reaping any benefits in this market," he said. "This has proven to be a formidable task."
Intel invented x86 chips and is successfully maintaining its top market position.
Just last Monday, the company shocked Wall Street with quarterly results that exceeded even analysts' recently raised estimates.
Intel's net income for its third quarter powered to $1.3 billion from $931 million a year earlier, as its revenue rose 23 percent to $5.1 billion for the September quarter alone.

Other companies in the "x86 market" include Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Cyrix Corp. -- both of which posted losses in the latest quarter -- while Motorola Inc., International Business Machines Corp. and Apple Computer Inc. have teamed up to develop and sell the rival PowerPC chip.
Dataquest noted the powerful upgrade cycle for personal computers, with new features requiring ever-faster machines helping maintain demand for the latest products.

"This market will continue to succeed because new applications will continue to drive demand for higher performance systems, with most users upgrading their systems every two-to-three years," Brookwood said.

The market for embedded microprocessors, in which special features are built into the device, is expected to grow at a compound rate of 12 percent through the year 2000, according to another Dataquest study to be released on Monday.
A smaller, more competitive market, the value of embedded microprocessors sold is due to reach $3.1 billion by 2000, up from $1.8 billion last year, Dataquest projected.

"Unlike the computer segment, which is effectively closed to new participants, the embedded market has the opportunity for a number of vendors and processors besides the 8086 derivatives," said Tom Starnes, director and analyst of Dataquest's Embedded Microcomponents Worldwide program.

The 8086 microprocessor is the first in the Intel series, which is now known more generically as the x86 market. For competitive reasons, Intel has moved away from its X86 naming: its current chips known as the Pentium and Pentium Pro models.

In contrast to CISC microprocessors, which are primarily used in PCs, embedded microchips are used in a broad range of applications ranging from telecommunications, printers and video games to automotive and industrial controls.
